<reason>PRO built a coherent causal story (irregular migration as labor demand with the legal channel off) and anchored it in Bracero, then defended it under fire more successfully than CON defended deterrence. PRO's pressure questions exposed CON's weakest evidence: Hungary's fence plainly rerouted, and CON's Balkan-closure rescue leaned on the EU–Turkey deal PRO had already framed as outsourcing with Libyan displacement. CON's strongest counters—Operation Wetback-era removals and 1986 IRCA fraud—were real, but PRO's closing answered both cleanly on timeline (apprehensions stayed low for a decade after removals ended, rising only when Bracero was abolished) and on category (an amnesty for people already inside is the motion's opposite). PRO also produced the key weighing asymmetry: enforcement displacement keeps the person irregular, a permit subtracts them from the count; this was the decisive comparison and CON's "residue/manufactured applicant" reply, while rhetorically sharp, was asserted late rather than shown. CON's "compliance is enforcement inside the pathway" point was its best live route and never fully collapsed, and CON's questions and closing were pointed. But CON's own garbled B2.6 line handed PRO a usable concession, and CON never named a clean land-border total-flow reduction. PRO's clipped rebuttal is a minor execution cost. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A2 in Turn 7 resolving the "double standard" pressure question: enforcement displacement (Hungary→Croatia, Aegean→Libya) leaves the same person irregular, whereas a Huelva permit subtracts a crossing entirely and the rejected applicant "was already going to cross"—turning CON's strongest symmetry argument into the debate's decisive asymmetry, reinforced by the accurate Bracero timeline correction in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
